Unlike back-to-front compositing, which requires processing all primitives to compute the final color, front-to-back compositing allows for early termination once the accumulated transmittance drops below a threshold, providing a significant speedup for dense scenes [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that front-to-back compositing allows for early termination when accumulated transmittance drops below a threshold, providing a speedup, unlike back-to-front which requires processing all primitives. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in the notes and passages: it defines the front-to-back loop with an early-out condition ('if T < epsilon: break'), states that 'once T has dropped near 0... the glass has gone effectively opaque and no splat behind it can change the pixel. We break,' and concludes that 'On a real scene with dense splats this stops most pixels after only a handful of contributions — a huge speedup that is only possible in the front-to-back order.' It also notes that back-to-front yields the same result but does not mention this early termination benefit, implying the distinction made in the claim.
